title: What Is AI, Really?
hook: Have you ever wondered how TikTok knows exactly which video will make you laugh, or how digital wallets like eSewa spot a fake transaction instantly? That is not magic. That is Artificial Intelligence (AI).
concept: AI is a computer program that learns from many examples. It finds patterns, then makes a good guess. Think of a local farmer predicting the monsoon. A farmer doesn't just guess; they look at the clouds, remember past weather patterns, and make a prediction. AI does something similar but instead of looking at the sky, it looks at data, like millions of past videos or financial records, to predict what you want to watch or if a payment is safe. AI is not a movie robot. It is a computer tool. Sometimes you can see it like a chatbot but it often works quietly in the background of your apps.

action.title: Think about your smartphone. Tap the app below where you think AI is working right now:

feedback.correct: Right! YouTube, digital wallets, and Maps all run on AI.
feedback.incorrect: True, but look closer: other options here use AI too.

quiz.title: Based on what you just read, what is AI?

options.label: A computer tool that finds patterns and makes guesses.

feedback.correct: Correct! Patterns, data, predictions. That is AI.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Remember the farmer. AI uses data to make predictions.

reward.message: Great job! You have taken your first step. See you tomorrow to uncover why AI chatbots aren't quite what they seem.

title: AI Doesn't “Think” Like You
hook: A chatbot says “I think” and “I feel.” It sounds like a friend. But is it?
concept:
Type “Dal Bhat Power, 24…” on your phone. The keyboard may suggest “Hour.” Did your phone understand the saying? No. It has seen those words together many times. So it guessed what comes next.
A chatbot does the same thing, but with a huge amount of text. It builds answers one word at a time using patterns. It has no feelings. It does not truly understand.
So be careful with words. “AI thinks” and “AI understands” are not quite right. Better words are “AI predicts” and “AI finds patterns.”

action.title: A student typed: “I failed my exam and feel like nobody cares.” The chatbot replied: “I'm so sorry to hear that. I truly understand how you feel.” Does the AI really feel sorry?

options.label: Yes, it feels sad for me
No, it is picking comforting words

feedback.correct: Right! It has no feelings. It just picks words that fit.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI has no feelings. It only matches patterns.

quiz.title: Which sentence describes AI best?

options.label: AI understands your feelings like a friend does.
AI predicts likely answers from patterns in data. It has no real feelings.
AI knows everything happening in the world right now.

feedback.correct: Correct! AI finds patterns. It does not have feelings.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: AI has no thoughts and no feelings. It matches patterns.

reward.message: Awesome! You now have better words for AI. Come back tomorrow to learn what to do when AI sounds sure but is wrong.

title: Can You Trust the Answer?
hook: A friend shows you a chatbot's homework answer. It sounds very sure. But sounding sure is not the same as being right.
concept:
AI predicts words from patterns. It does not check if something is true. So it can make mistakes and still sound sure. Sometimes it even makes up facts that are not real.
Before you use an AI answer, pick one: accept it, revise it, or reject it.
Accept: You checked it, and it is correct.
Revise: Part of it is right. You fix the mistake.
Reject: It is wrong. Do not use it.
To check, use your textbook, your teacher or a trusted source. Or do the work yourself.

action.title: Student: How many provinces does Nepal have? AI: Nepal has 5 provinces. Is the AI's answer correct?

feedback.correct: Correct! Nepal has 7 provinces. Always check answers that sound sure.
feedback.incorrect: Actually, Nepal has 7 provinces. AI can sound sure and still be wrong.

quiz.title: An AI gives you a fact for your homework. What should you do first?

options.label: Check it with a textbook, a teacher or a trusted source.
Trust it if it sounds sure.

feedback.correct: Yes! Check first, then decide.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Sounding sure does not mean it is true. Check it first.

reward.message: Awesome! You are now an AI fact-checker. Come back tomorrow to find out why your video feed seems to know you.

title: Why Does My Feed Know Me So Well?
hook: You watch two cricket videos. Suddenly your whole feed is full of cricket. Coincidence?
concept:
Apps like YouTube and TikTok use AI to suggest videos. They use data about you. This includes what you watch, like and search, and how long you stay on each video.
The AI finds patterns in that data. Then it guesses what you will click next. It does not know you as a person. It only uses data about your past choices.
This can help you find songs and videos you love. But it can also make your world smaller. Imagine a shopkeeper who only shows you what you bought before. You may never find something new.

action.title: Sita only watches cricket and momo videos. Which video will her feed most likely show next?

feedback.correct: Yes! The AI guesses from her past data. She watches a lot of cricket, so she will probably see more.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Sita has not watched or searched for anything like this. The AI has no pattern to follow. Try again!

quiz.title: Which of these can a video app use to recommend videos to you?

options.label: What you watch, like and search
The same videos for every user

feedback.correct: Yes! AI uses data about you to predict what you may enjoy.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI cannot read your thoughts. Videos are not the same for everyone. They come from data about you. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You now know why your feed looks the way it does. Tomorrow: what does it cost the planet when AI answers a question?

title: The Hidden Cost of a Chatbot Reply
hook: Your phone is at 5% and you panic. You hunt for the charger like it is treasure. Does AI ever get that hungry?
concept:
AI is not magic. It is software, and software runs on real computers. Computers need electricity, just like your phone. So every AI reply, even a small one, uses a little energy.
This does not mean you should stop using AI. But for easy jobs, ask: “Do I really need AI here, or can I do this myself?”
It is like walking to a nearby shop to save fuel. You do not need a vehicle for a short trip.

action.title: Which of these does a chatbot need to work?

options.label: Nothing, it floats in the air

feedback.correct: Yes! Every AI answer runs on real machines that use electricity.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI is not magic. It runs on real computers that need electricity and cooling. Try again!

quiz.title: What is one hidden cost of using AI?

options.label: AI makes your phone battery last longer.
AI uses real electricity and water in data centers.
AI has no environmental impact at all.

feedback.correct: Correct! Every reply uses real electricity and real water.
feedback.incorrect: Remember: every AI reply runs on real machines that use real resources.

reward.message: Nice! Be mindful, not scared. Come back tomorrow to find out if AI can be unfair. 🤔

title: Can AI Be Unfair?
hook: Imagine someone describes you using only your height and your favourite colour. Is that really you? 🤔 AI learns from data like this. So can it be fair to everyone?
concept:
AI finds patterns in data. People choose that data.
If the data leaves some people out, or is unfair, AI can copy the same unfairness. This is called bias.
Here is an example. AI often has much more English to read than Nepali. So it can be weaker with Nepali words, names and places.
Data also never tells the whole story. It can show your height, but not your kindness or your dreams.
So people must check AI, and not just trust it.

action.title: Maya's data card says: Height: 150 cm. Favourite colour: red. What is missing from this data?

feedback.correct: Yes! Data captures only a small part of a person. Always ask: who or what is left out?
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That is already on the card. Think about what numbers and colours cannot show. Try again!

quiz.title: Why can AI be unfair?

options.label: It copies patterns from data that may be unfair or leave people out

feedback.correct: Yes! AI copies patterns from data, and that data may be unfair or leave people out.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI does not choose to be mean. Unfair or missing data can make AI unfair. Try again!

reward.message: Tomorrow we finish Week 1. How do you decide if a way of using AI is okay?

title: Is It Fair to Use AI This Way?
hook: An AI makes a painting in the style of a Mithila artist. The artist spent years learning that art. Is it fair?
concept:
AI is a tool. Using it can be fair or unfair. It depends on how the AI was made and why you use it.
How it was made matters. What data did it learn from? Did the artists agree?
Think of the Mithila artist. Someone uses AI to copy the style. They sell the pictures without credit. This can hurt the artist.
Before you use AI, ask: Is it honest? Is it fair? Who could be hurt?

action.title: A student uses AI to copy a Mithila artist's style and sells the pictures without telling anyone. What is the most important question to ask?

options.label: Is it fair to the artist?

feedback.correct: Yes! Fairness to the people behind the work is the key question.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Colours and speed don't tell us if it is fair. Think about the artist. Try again!

quiz.title: Fair use of AI depends on:

options.label: How the AI was made, and why you use it

feedback.correct: Yes! How it was made and your reason both matter.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Both parts matter: how the AI was made and why you use it. Try again!

reward.message: Week 1 complete! You are not just using AI now. You are asking questions about it, checking it and using it fairly. Come back next week to Create with AI!

review.title: Week 1 Revision Quiz: True or False? Tap one for each statement.

questions.statement: AI can work quietly in the background of your apps.

feedback.correct: Right! You don't always see AI, but it is often working behind the scenes.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI is often hidden in the background, like in video recommendations and maps.

questions.statement: A chatbot understands your feelings like a friend.

feedback.correct: Right! A chatbot predicts words from patterns. It has no feelings.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A chatbot can sound caring, but it only predicts words from patterns. It has no feelings or understanding.

questions.statement: If AI sounds sure, you do not need to check its answer.

feedback.correct: Right! AI can sound sure and still be wrong, so check, then accept, revise or reject.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Sounding sure doesn't make it correct. Always check first.

questions.statement: Video apps use data about what you watch, like and search to recommend videos.

feedback.correct: Right! AI uses data about you to predict what you may enjoy.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Recommendations come from data about your clicks, likes and searches.

questions.statement: AI works without electricity because it is only software.

feedback.correct: Right! Software runs on real computers, which need electricity and cooling.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. No electricity means no computers, and no computers means no AI.

questions.statement: AI can be unfair if the data it learns from is unfair or leaves people out.

feedback.correct: Right! Unfair data can lead to unfair results.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI finds patterns in data, so unfair or incomplete data can make it unfair.

questions.statement: Fair use of AI depends only on the AI tool, not on the user.

feedback.correct: Right! It depends on how the AI was made and on why you use it.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Why you use AI matters too, along with how it was made.

title: Your Idea First, AI Second
hook: You are writing a story about a jungle. Nice, but a bit ordinary. Now imagine the jungle is in space. One twist, and the story gets exciting!
concept:
Great ideas start with you. First, think of your own idea, even a small one.
Then AI can help you find more ideas. Ask it for twists, questions or “what if” ideas. Its ideas can surprise you and help you think in new ways.
But AI does not replace your idea. It only gives suggestions. You decide what to keep, change or drop.

action.title: Your idea is a story about a farmer. Which question to AI will give the best new ideas?

options.label: “Give me 3 surprising twists for my story about a farmer.”

feedback.correct: Yes! Your idea comes first, and AI sparks new directions.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That asks AI to replace your idea. Ask for twists or “what if” questions instead. Try again!

quiz.title: AI suggests “a jungle in space” for your story. What should you do?

options.label: Use it exactly as it is
Decide what to keep, change or drop to fit your idea

feedback.correct: Yes! You are the creator. AI only gives suggestions.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Your idea matters most. Look at the suggestion, then decide what fits your story. Try again!

reward.message: Good thinking! Your idea comes first, and AI helps it grow. Come back tomorrow to mix AI's ideas with yours, not replace them.

title: Remix, Don't Replace
hook: You love momo. AI suggests pizza. Mix them and you get momo pizza! That is a remix. It is how new ideas are born.
concept:
A good creator follows three steps:
Think first. Write your own ideas before you ask AI.
Compare. Ask AI for ideas. Then put them next to yours. What is the same? What is different?
Remix. Take the best parts of both and make something new.
Be careful. AI's idea may look great and make yours feel small. But your idea still counts. You decide what to keep, change or drop.

action.title: AI suggests three story endings. Which choice is a real “remix”?

options.label: Copy the ending you like best, word for word
Take the best idea from two endings and write it in your own words and style

feedback.correct: Right! That is a real remix, in your own voice.
feedback.incorrect: That is just copying. Try mixing ideas in your own words.

quiz.title: What does it mean to “remix” an AI suggestion?

options.label: Say no to every suggestion AI makes.
Take the useful parts and change them with your own voice and thinking.
Copying the AI's exact words to save time.

feedback.correct: Correct! Remixing means changing ideas with your own voice.
feedback.incorrect: Remixing is not all or nothing. You pick the useful parts and change them.

reward.message: Nicely done! Remixing keeps you in charge of your own work. Tomorrow: what happens when AI turns your words into a picture?

title: Turning Words Into Pictures
hook: Close your eyes. Picture a goat wearing sunglasses on a grassy ground. Now imagine typing those words and watching the picture appear. That is what AI image tools do!
concept:
An AI image maker turns your words into a picture. The words you type are called a prompt.
Details in your prompt change the result. “A goat” gives a plain picture. “A goat wearing sunglasses on a grassy ground” is much closer to your idea.
AI cannot see the picture in your mind. It only uses your words. So after it makes a picture, check it. What matches your idea? What is wrong? Then change your words and try again.

action.title: You want a picture of a happy village festival. Which prompt will give the closest result?

options.label: “A happy village festival at night with colourful lights, people dancing, cartoon style”

feedback.correct: Yes! It has who, where and style, so the AI has more to work with.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Too few details. AI cannot see your idea, so tell it who, where and what style. Try again!

quiz.title: AI makes a picture, but it is not what you imagined. What is the best next step?

options.label: Accept it, because AI made it
Compare it with your idea, then change your words and try again

feedback.correct: Yes! The first picture is a first try. Compare it, change your words and try again.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Check whether the picture matches your idea, then change your prompt. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You can now turn your words into pictures. Come back tomorrow for the next step.

title: If AI Can Draw It, Can AI Fake It?
hook: A photo of a flooded bridge goes viral. Your family shares it. But the flood never happened. Someone made that picture with AI.
concept:
AI can make more than words. It can make pictures, voices and videos too. Some look so real that it is hard to tell what is fake.
A fake picture, voice or video that looks real is called a deepfake.
Looking closely is not enough to catch a fake. Instead, check the source. Who posted it? Do trusted news sources report it?
And never use AI to make fakes that could trick or hurt people.

action.title: A photo of a flooded bridge is going viral. It looks real. What should you do first?

options.label: Share it fast so people stay safe
Check who posted it and whether trusted news reports it
Trust it because it looks real

feedback.correct: Yes! Check the source before you share.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A picture that looks real can still be fake. Check who posted it and whether trusted news reports it first. Try again!

quiz.title: What is the safest habit when you see a shocking photo or video online?

options.label: Forward it right away, just in case it is true.
Check it with a trusted source before you believe or share it.
Only forward it if it is about someone you do not like.

feedback.correct: Correct! Check first, especially before you share.
feedback.incorrect: Being fast is not being safe. Always check shocking things before you act.

reward.message: This is one of the most important habits in this course. These tricks often target parents and grandparents, so teach this to your family tonight. Tomorrow: how do you get useful feedback from AI, not just empty praise?

title: Getting Better Feedback
hook: You show your drawing to a friend. They say, “Nice.” Is that helpful? Not really. You want to know what works and what to fix. AI feedback is the same. A better question gets better feedback.
concept:
AI can give feedback on your idea, but it only knows what you tell it. Compare two prompts for the same poem:
Prompt 1: “Is my poem good?”
Prompt 2: “I am in Class 7. I wrote a 4-line poem about the monsoon. Tell me 2 things that work and 1 thing to improve, in simple words.”
Prompt 2 gets better feedback. It tells who you are and what you wrote (context). It says what you want (specific). It sets limits (2 things, 1 thing, simple words).
Same idea, different prompt, different answer. Share your idea, not private things like your address or phone number.

action.title: You ask AI, “Is my story good?” Which change will get more useful feedback?

options.label: Add who you are, what the story is about, and what kind of feedback you want

feedback.correct: Yes! Context, details and a clear request give AI more to work with.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Those do not give the AI more useful information. Add context, details and the kind of feedback you want. Try again!

quiz.title: AI replies, “Your poem is nice.” That does not help. What is the best next step?

options.label: Ask again: “I am in Class 7. Give me 2 things that work and 1 thing to improve, in simple words.”
Ask the exact same question again

feedback.correct: Yes! A clearer prompt gets more useful feedback.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A vague question gets vague feedback. Add context and details, then try again!

reward.message: Well done! Better questions get better feedback. Come back tomorrow to find out whose work it is when AI makes something.

title: Whose Work Is It Anyway?
hook: Say AI writes a song “in the style of” a famous singer. Who owns it? The singer, the AI company, or the person who typed the request?
concept:
AI finds patterns in huge amounts of data. This includes songs, pictures and writing made by real people.
Some of that work is protected by copyright. Copyright is a law. It protects what creators make, so others cannot copy it freely.
So AI-made content may copy a creator's work. That matters to the person who made the original. Their effort, their credit and sometimes their money are at risk.

action.title: A friend uses AI to make a song that sounds just like a famous singer. They post it as their own. What is the biggest problem?

options.label: Nothing. AI made it, so nobody's work was used
It may copy the singer's work, and the singer gets no credit

feedback.correct: Yes! AI learns from real people's work, so the singer's effort and credit matter.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI-made content can copy real people's work. Think about the singer. Try again!

quiz.title: When AI-made content copies a creator's work, who can be affected?

options.label: The creator who made the original

feedback.correct: Yes! Their effort, credit and sometimes income are affected.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Real people made the original work, and they can lose credit or income. Try again!

reward.message: Thoughtful work! Respecting creators is part of using AI well. Tomorrow we finish Week 2. Time to show what you can make.

title: Show What You Made (+ Week 2 Review)
hook: This week you learned to spark ideas, remix, write prompts, spot fakes, ask for feedback and respect creators. Now it's your turn to make something!
concept:
Pick one: a poster about something you care about, the start of a short story, or a 4-line poem. Then follow these steps:
1. Idea first. Write your own idea in one line.
2. Prompt. Write a prompt with context, details and limits.
3. Check. Does the result match your idea? What surprised you? Could any part be wrong or fake?
4. Remix. Keep, change or drop parts of it to fit your idea.
5. Think of the creator. Could it copy someone's work?
No AI tool? No problem. Write the prompt you would use and imagine what AI might make. If you do use a tool, use it with a teacher or parent.

action.title: You start your mini-project. What is the first step?

options.label: Write your own idea in one line

feedback.correct: Yes! Your idea comes first, and AI helps it grow.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Think of your own idea first, then ask AI to spark more. Try again!

quiz.title: AI gives you a poster that looks great, but you're not sure it is right or original. What should you do?

options.label: Use it right away, because it looks great
Check it against your idea, then keep, change or drop parts, and think about whether it copies someone's work
Throw away your idea and use AI's

feedback.correct: Yes! Check it, remix it, and think of the creator.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Looking great doesn't make it right or original. Check it, remix it so it fits your idea, and think about whose work it might copy. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You planned your own creation. Next: take the Week 2 Quiz to lock in what you learned!

title: Which AI Tool Fits Which Job?
hook: AI can summarise a long lesson in seconds. But can it cheer up a sad friend?
concept:
There are many kinds of AI tools. Each is made for certain jobs. Some summarise long texts. Some make pictures. Some translate. Some spot patterns, like a maps app that finds traffic.
But AI has no feelings. It does not truly understand your situation. So it fits some tasks better than others. Other tools fit too. A search engine is good for research. A calculator is good for sums.
Before you start, ask: What is my task? Which tool fits it? What do my teacher and school say about AI? And never share private details with an AI tool.

action.title: Your teacher says, “Use AI to summarise, and a search engine for research.” You need to summarise a long chapter. Which tool fits best?

feedback.correct: Yes! Summarising long text is a job AI tools are made for. Match the tool to the task.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That tool is built for a different job. Match the tool to the task. Try again!

quiz.title: Which of these is a task AI tools are designed to support?

feedback.correct: Yes! AI can support tasks like summarising, spotting patterns and making content.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI has no feelings and does not truly understand. Tools like summarisers are made to summarise text. Try again!

reward.message: Good thinking! You can now match the right tool to the task. Tomorrow: what do you do when something online promises too much?

title: Do I Even Need AI For This?
hook: AI can write a thank-you note to your grandmother in five seconds. But should it?
concept:
Yesterday you matched AI tools to jobs. Today you decide: should AI do this task at all? Put every task in one of four buckets:
AI Only: AI can do it well and nothing important is lost. Example: finding the fastest route on a maps app.
AI-Supported: AI helps, but you lead. Example: getting poster ideas from AI, then choosing the best one.
Human Only: it needs your feelings, your own thinking or your own learning. Example: a thank-you note to someone you care about. Or your teacher says no AI.
Not Sure: ask your teacher.
To choose, ask: Is this a job AI tools are made for? Does it need my feelings or my own thinking? What do my teacher and school say?

action.title: Task: get ideas for your poster, then you pick the best one and draw it. Which bucket?

feedback.correct: Yes! AI helps with ideas, but you choose and make the poster.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI can help with ideas, but you choose and make the poster. That's AI-Supported. Try again!

quiz.title: Your teacher says, “No AI for today's essay.” Which bucket?

feedback.correct: Yes! Your teacher's rules come first. This task is Human Only.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. When your teacher says no AI, the task is Human Only. Always follow your teacher's and school's rules. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You can now sort tasks: AI Only, AI-Supported or Human Only. Tomorrow: what is the difference between AI that follows fixed rules and AI that learns from examples?

title: Rules vs. Learning: Two Kinds of AI
hook: Imagine two ways to sort vegetables at a kirana pasal. One person follows a strict list of rules. Another person has learned by watching thousands of examples. Both get the job done, but in very different ways.
concept:
Some AI follows fixed rules that a person wrote. For example: “If it is green and long, call it a cucumber.”
Other AI learns from many examples. It finds patterns in thousands of photos or records. Nobody tells it exact rules.
Rule-based AI struggles with anything unusual. Learning-based AI is more flexible and handles new things better. But it can make surprising mistakes on things it has not seen much.
Neither type is “better.” Each one fits different jobs.

action.title: A robot sorts trash using one instruction: “If a magnet sticks, it is metal.” Which type is it?

feedback.correct: Yes! It follows an exact instruction written by a person.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. This robot follows an exact instruction written by a person. That is a rules-based system. Try again!

quiz.title: Which system finds patterns in data?

options.label: A robot that follows a list of rules
A system trained on thousands of photos of paper, plastic and metal

feedback.correct: Yes! It learns from examples and uses patterns to sort new items.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Lists of rules and calculators follow instructions written by people. The system that finds patterns is trained on lots of examples. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You now know AI can follow rules or find patterns. Come back tomorrow for the next step.

title: Which Way Fits the Job?
hook: A simple traffic light follows a timer. A translation app learns from examples. Why not use the same way for both?
concept:
Yesterday you learned two ways AI can work: rules, and patterns from data. Today: when is each one better?
Rules (like a calculator or a simple traffic light)
✅ Same answer every time, and easy to check
❌ Gets stuck when no rule covers the problem. Hard to write for messy tasks
Patterns from data (like translation or photo recognition)
✅ Can handle messy tasks that have too many cases for rules
❌ Needs lots of examples. Can be wrong or unfair. Harder to explain
So pick by the task. An exact, simple task suits rules. A messy task with lots of examples suits patterns.

action.title: Which task suits a rules-based way best?

options.label: Translating a Nepali poem into English
Adding two numbers on a calculator
Recognising a friend's face in photos

feedback.correct: Yes! It is exact and simple, so the rules work perfectly.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That task is too messy for a short list of rules. Adding numbers is exact, so rules work best. Try again!

quiz.title: Which is a drawback of a rules-based system?

options.label: It can get stuck when something isn't covered by a rule
It needs thousands of examples to learn
It cannot give the same answer twice

feedback.correct: Yes! Rules only cover what people think of.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Needing many examples is a problem for pattern-learning AI. Rules give the same answer every time. The drawback of rules is that they get stuck in new situations. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You can now say when rules or patterns fit a task better. Tomorrow: what kind of problem is it?

title: What Kind of Problem Is It?
hook: Predicting tomorrow's weather. Comforting a sad friend. Designing a poster. Are they the same kind of problem? Not at all!
concept:
Before you use AI, ask: what kind of problem is this? Here are three common types:
Data-based: it needs patterns in lots of information, like predicting the weather. AI can often help.
Emotional: it needs feelings, care and understanding, like comforting a friend. AI cannot feel, so a person should lead.
Creative: it needs new ideas, like designing a poster. AI can spark ideas, but you decide and create.
So is AI always needed? No. Some problems are best solved by you.

action.title: What type of problem is “predicting tomorrow's weather”?

feedback.correct: Yes! Weather prediction uses patterns in lots of data.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Weather prediction depends on patterns in lots of data, so it is a data-based problem. Try again!

quiz.title: Your friend is sad after failing a test. What type of problem is this, and who should lead?

options.label: Emotional, and you should lead with care

feedback.correct: Yes! Feelings need a caring person. AI cannot feel or truly understand.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Sadness is an emotional problem. AI has no feelings, so a caring person should lead. Try again!

reward.message: Great! You can now name the type of problem before you reach for AI. Tomorrow: how to stay in charge of AI.

title: You Stay in Charge
hook: A cricket coach uses AI to study every player's moves. But who picks the final team? The coach does! AI helps, and the human decides.
concept:
AI is used in sports, news, music and schools. In every case, a person must stay in charge.
When you use AI, follow three rules:
Accountability: You are responsible for what you use and share. If AI is wrong, it is still your work.
Learning: Use AI to help you learn, not to skip learning.
Fairness: Say that you used AI. Follow your teacher's rules. Never use AI to cheat or hurt others.

action.title: Which choice shows responsible AI use?

options.label: Ask AI to write your whole essay and hand it in
Use AI for ideas if your teacher allows it, write the essay yourself, and say you used AI
Use AI, but hide it from your teacher

feedback.correct: Yes! You do the learning, you are honest, and you follow your teacher's rules.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Responsible use means you do the learning, you are honest about AI, and you follow your teacher's rules. Try again!

quiz.title: Your school project used AI, and it contained a mistake. Who is responsible?

feedback.correct: Yes! AI is a tool. You are responsible for what you use and share.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI is a tool and cannot be held responsible. You are responsible for what you use and share. Try again!

reward.message: Well done! You are always the one in charge. Tomorrow we finish Week 3 by putting this into practice.

title: Plan a Human+AI Task Together (+ Week 3 Review)
hook: Time to plan like a pro! 🤝 You will plan one task where you and AI each do the right part.
concept:
Pick one task: a poster for a school clean-up day, a 2-minute talk about a local festival, or the start of a short story. Then plan it:
1. Name the problem type. Is it data-based, emotional or creative?
2. Match the tool. Is this a job AI tools are built for? Which tool fits?
3. Decide who leads. AI Only, AI-Supported or Human Only? Check your teacher's rules first.
4. Stay in charge. How will you take responsibility for what you share, keep learning, and be honest about using AI?
No AI tool? No problem. Just write your plan. If you do use a tool, use it with a teacher or parent.

action.title: You plan a poster for a school clean-up day. What type of problem is it?

feedback.correct: Yes! A poster needs new ideas, so it is a creative problem. AI can spark ideas, but you create.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A poster needs new ideas, which makes it a creative problem. Try again!

quiz.title: Your teacher allows AI for ideas. Your plan: AI gives poster ideas, you pick one and draw it, and you tell your teacher you used AI. What is this plan?

feedback.correct: Yes! AI helps, and you lead, learn and stay honest.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. AI helps with ideas, but you choose and draw the poster. That is AI-Supported. Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You planned a task where you and AI each do the right part. Next: take the Week 3 Quiz to lock in what you learned!

title: The AI ID Card
hook: Every medicine has a label that tells you what it is for and what to avoid. Should AI have one too?
concept:
Every AI system is built by people for a certain job. A maps app finds routes. A translator changes languages. A chatbot predicts words. People decide what each one is for.
So how do you know what an AI system is designed to do? Read its ID card. Experts call it a model card. It tells you:
Job: what it is designed to do
Learned from: the data it was trained on
Limits: what it is not good at
Use AI for its job, not for jobs it was never built to do.

action.title:
Read this ID card:
PhotoSort
Job: Sorts photos by what is in them (people, food, animals)
Learned from: 1 million labelled photos
Limits: Not good with dark or blurry photos

What is PhotoSort designed to do?

options.label: Sort photos by what is in them

feedback.correct: Yes! The Job line tells you what an AI is designed to do.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Read the Job line again. PhotoSort sorts photos by what is in them. Try again!

quiz.title: Using the same ID card, when is PhotoSort NOT a good choice?

feedback.correct: Yes! The Limits line says it is not good with dark or blurry photos.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The card says PhotoSort sorts food and animals. Its limit is dark or blurry photos. Try again!

reward.message: Excellent! You can now read an AI's ID card. Tomorrow: become an AI detective and investigate any AI tool!

title: Be an AI Detective
hook: A hiking app finds great routes for hikers. But what if a cyclist in a busy city uses it? Would it still work?
concept:
Yesterday you read an AI's ID card. Today you investigate like a detective. Ask four questions about any AI tool:
Purpose: What is its main job?
Made for: Who is it designed for?
Input → Output: What goes in, and what comes out?
Limits: Where does it struggle?
Try it on a chatbot. Its purpose is answering questions in text. It is made for people who can read and type. The input is your question, and the output is words it predicts. Its limit is that it can be wrong, even when it sounds sure.

action.title:
Read this ID card:
TrekGuide
Purpose: Suggests safe walking routes on mountain trails
Made for: Trekkers
Input → Output: Start point, destination and weather data → a suggested route
Limits: Does not know about trails closed today

What is the input for TrekGuide?

options.label: Start point, destination and weather data

feedback.correct: Yes! Input is what goes in. Output is what comes out.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Input is what goes in: the start point, destination and weather data. The route is what comes out. Try again!

quiz.title: Is TrekGuide a good fit for a cyclist riding in a busy city?

options.label: Yes, a route is a route
No, it was made for trekkers on mountain trails
Yes, because it uses weather data

feedback.correct: Yes! Check Purpose and Made for. City roads are outside what it was designed for.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. TrekGuide was designed for trekkers on mountain trails. A tool may not work well for people it wasn't made for. Try again!

reward.message: Good work! You can now investigate any AI tool like a detective. Tomorrow: how do you know if an AI did a good job?

title: Did the AI Do a Good Job?
hook: A music app suggests 5 songs for you. 🎵 Is that a win? It depends on what “win” means. Decide first, then judge!
concept:
How do you know if an AI did a good job? Decide what success looks like before you check. This list is called your criteria.
For a music AI, the criteria could be:
The songs match what the listener likes.
A few songs are new, so the listener can discover more.
The songs are suitable for the listener's age.
Good criteria are clear. You can answer Yes or No to each one. “The songs are good” is too vague.
And different listeners like different things, so check the AI's picks for different people.

action.title: Which is the best success criterion for a music AI?

options.label: The songs match what the listener likes

feedback.correct: Yes! It is clear and you can check it with Yes or No.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That is vague or not about the AI's job. A good criterion is clear and checkable, like “the songs match what the listener likes.” Try again!

quiz.title: Asha loves Nepali folk songs. Ram loves rock. The AI gives both of them the same 5 pop songs. Did it succeed?

options.label: No, the songs don't match their different tastes

feedback.correct: Yes! Your first criterion is that songs match the listener's taste. Asha and Ram like different things, so the same pop list fails them.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Check your criteria: songs should match what each listener likes. Asha and Ram have different tastes, so the same list fails. Try again!

reward.message: Nice! You can now define what success looks like for an AI. Tomorrow: put an AI to the test and score it!

title: Put the AI to the Test
hook: Your friend says, “This new AI is the best ever!” Do you believe it? Not until you test it!
concept:
Yesterday you set criteria for success. Today you use them to test an AI in three steps:
Criteria: Write your checklist first.
Test: Try the AI on many examples, easy and tricky. These are your test cases. One good result can be luck.
Score and ask: Mark each criterion Yes or No for every test. Then ask real people what they think. This is user feedback.
You can also use a benchmark test. It is a fixed set of questions with known answers, like a quiz with an answer key. It lets you compare AI systems fairly.

action.title: You want to test a maths helper AI. Which test is best?

options.label: Ask 10 questions, easy and tricky, and check each answer against an answer key
Ask the AI if it is correct

feedback.correct: Yes! Many test cases and an answer key give a fair result.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. One test can be lucky, and AI can sound sure even when it is wrong (Day 3). Use many test cases and check each answer against a key. Try again!

quiz.title: The maths AI got 8 of 10 questions right. Three students said its steps were confusing. What is the best conclusion?

options.label: It is good at correct answers but needs improvement on clear steps

feedback.correct: Yes! You checked each criterion. The test shows strengths, and the students' feedback shows a weakness.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. 8 of 10 is good for correct answers, but students found the steps unclear. A fair result shows both strengths and weaknesses. Try again!

reward.message: Awesome! You can now test an AI and score it. Tomorrow: what does AI learn from? Pick the data to train your own AI!

title: What Does AI Learn From?
hook: You want to build an AI that tells ripe mangoes from unripe ones. You can't just tell it. You have to show it the right data. Which data would you pick?
concept:
AI learns from data: photos, text, sounds and numbers. Data comes from many places:
Public information, like websites and books
What people post, like photos and videos
Sensors, like cameras, microphones and GPS
Carefully built collections, like a set of photos with labels
People choose this data, sort it and label it. For the mango AI, you would collect photos of ripe and unripe mangoes, each labelled. Photos of cars would not help.
Data about people should only be used with their permission.

action.title: You want to train an AI to tell ripe mangoes from unripe ones. Which data helps most?

options.label: Labelled photos of ripe and unripe mangoes

feedback.correct: Yes! The data must match the task, and the labels tell the AI which is which.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. The data must match the task. For mangoes, you need labelled photos of ripe and unripe mangoes. Try again!

quiz.title: A camera on a farm records photos of crops every day. What kind of data source is this?

feedback.correct: Yes! Cameras, microphones and GPS collect data automatically.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. Photos are data, and a camera collects them automatically. That makes it a sensor. Try again!

reward.message: Woah! You can now spot the data an AI learns from. Tomorrow: how can we make AI better for everyone?

title: Make AI Better for Everyone
hook: An AI helper only uses long, hard English words. 😕 Many students and grandparents give up. Can we fix that? Yes! People built it, and people can improve it.
concept:
People design AI, so people can change it. Simple changes can make an AI tool helpful for more people:
Clearer instructions that are easy to follow
Answers that suit the user's age
Options for different needs, like a Nepali language choice, or a voice reader for people who find reading hard
AI can be made to help people, communities and the planet.
It can help one person, like a study helper. It can help a village, like a weather alert. It can help the planet, like a tool that helps farmers save water.
For any change, ask: Who would benefit, and why?

action.title: A homework-helper AI uses long, hard English words. Class 6 students and elderly readers struggle. Which change helps most?

options.label: Use simple words and add a Nepali language option

feedback.correct: Yes! Simple words and a language option make the tool useful for more people.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That would make it harder for more people to use. Simple words and a language option help more people. Try again!

quiz.title: Who would benefit from adding a voice reader to an AI tool?

options.label: People who find reading hard, such as some learners and elderly users

feedback.correct: Yes! Improving AI for different needs helps more people.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. A voice reader helps people who find reading hard. Thinking about who benefits is the first step in improving AI. Try again!

reward.message: Great! You now know AI can be improved for people, communities and the planet. Tomorrow: your final Week 4 review!

title: Design Your Own AI (+ Week 4 Review)
hook: Final day! 🎓 Today you design your own AI, on paper. You'll be the one who shapes it.
concept:
Plan an AI helper for your school that finds study resources or shares notices on time. Fill in its ID card:
1. Job and Made for: What is its main job? Who is it designed for?
2. Learned from: What data would train it? Where would the data come from?
3. Success checklist: Write 2 clear criteria you can check with Yes or No.
4. Test plan: How will you test it on many examples? Who will you ask for feedback?
5. Make it better for everyone: Add one change that helps more people, like a Nepali language option. Who would benefit, and why?
No AI tool needed. Just plan it on paper or in a note.

action.title: Which is the best success criterion for your school AI helper?

options.label: A student can find the right study resource, and you can check it with Yes or No

feedback.correct: Yes! A good criterion is clear and checkable.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. That is vague or not about the AI's job. A good criterion is clear and can be checked with Yes or No (Day 24). Try again!

quiz.title: Before your school helper goes live, how should you test it?

options.label: Try it on one easy question
Try it on many easy and tricky examples, and ask students for feedback
Ask the AI if it works

feedback.correct: Yes! Many test cases and real feedback give a fair result.
feedback.incorrect: Not quite. One result can be lucky, and an AI cannot judge itself fairly. Use many test cases and ask real users (Day 25). Try again!

reward.message: Nicely done! You designed your own AI helper. Next: take the Week 4 Quiz for your final check!
